---
title: 'Advantages of Programmatic Approaches'
---

Everything in Units 1 and 2 used browser-based tools: [Teachable Machine](../unit_1/teachable_machine.qmd), [Hack Merlin](../unit_1/hack_merlin.qmd), [Gemini Notebook](../unit_2/gemini_notebook.qmd), and chat assistants. They were easy to start with, and they produced real results. In the [Gemini Notebook activity](../unit_2/gemini_notebook.qmd), you found the people, places, and organizations in 20 letters, and got a data file back.

So why write code at all? Not because code is inherently better. The model you'll run in this unit is, on these letters, *less* accurate than Gemini Notebook was. The reason to use code is **control**: over *what* is done to your data, *how* it is done, *by which model*, and just as importantly, over *whether you can do it again* and expect the same results.

## Control, Not Capability

On the eight letters that two people annotated, here is how Gemini Notebook compares with the pre-trained NER model you'll use in the [case study](ner_case_study.qmd), measured by F1 (the [balance of precision and recall](../unit_1/evaluation_metrics.qmd#f1-score)):

<div class="table-container table-50">

| Entity type | Gemini (run 1) | Gemini (run 2) | NER model |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| People | 0.76 | 0.74 | 0.57 |
| Places | 0.82 | 0.78 | 0.68 |
| Organizations | 0.72 | 0.72 | 0.40 |
: {.sm}

</div>

Gemini Notebook wins on accuracy, clearly. Now compare what else each gives you:

<div class="table-container">

| | Gemini Notebook | The NER pipeline |
|--|---|---|
| **Same input, same output?** | No: two runs shared only ~88% of their rows | Yes: identical every time |
| **Can you see the method?** | No: the code Gemini ran wasn't shown, and its description of the steps didn't reproduce the results | Yes: every step is in the notebook |
| **Which model?** | Not shown, and it changes without notice | Named, with a published model card, and a library version you can record |
| **All of your documents?** | Hard to verify which documents, or which parts of them, were used | One row per entity, from every file, and you can count them |
| **What the output looks like** | Whatever the tool decided this time | Columns you defined, the same every time |
| **Where your data lives** | Google's servers | Your computer, or a Colab session you control |
| **Can you rerun it in five years?** | Only if the product, the model, and your account still exist | Yes, if you keep the code, the model, and the library versions |
: {.sm}

</div>

None of this is a criticism of Gemini Notebook. It's genuinely good at exploration and interpretation. The limits come from the format: a conversation with a product that someone else runs and changes.

For research, those limits often matter more than a few points of accuracy. A result you can't reproduce, inspect, or describe exactly is hard to build on, check, or publish. And a less accurate method whose accuracy you have *measured* is often more useful than a more accurate one you can't pin down. Measuring it is what the last two activities in this unit are for.

## The Case for Code

Coding has a real cost: setting up an environment, learning some syntax, debugging. So the useful question isn't <span class="quote">Should I learn to code?</span> but rather <span class="quote">What do I need code for?</span> Here are some typical signs that a task needs it:

- You need to process more material than a tool will accept, or more than you could check by hand, and have the certainty that all of it was processed.
- You need output you can count, sort, filter, map, or feed into another analysis, in a format you control.
- You need to be able to rerun the same process later, on new data, or for a reviewer.
- You need to know exactly what was done to every document.
- You are working with material that shouldn't leave your computer or your institution.

If none of these apply, a conversational tool may be all you need, as long as you [check its output](../unit_2/assessing_reliability.qmd) and [record what you did](../unit_2/documenting_ai_use.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## The Best of Both Worlds

The choice isn't strictly between a chat window and a small specialized model. There are approaches in-between, which you may find, or want, once you're comfortable with this unit:

- **Calling an LLM from code.** Instead of typing into a chat window, a script sends each document to a model through the provider's API (*Application Programming Interface*), with a saved prompt, and saves every response. You can name an exact model version, process every file the same way, and evaluate the results exactly as you'll evaluate the NER model here. You keep the flexibility of an LLM, and gain much of the control of a pipeline. **Two caveats:** the output can still vary between runs, and providers retire old model versions, so you can't rerun it forever.
- **Running an open model on your own computer.** Some LLMs can be downloaded and run locally, with tools built for the purpose. Your data never leaves your machine, and the model never changes unless you change it. They are usually smaller and less capable than the models behind commercial chat assistants.
- **Building your own retrieval.** Gemini Notebook uses [retrieval-augmented generation](../unit_2/prompts.qmd#the-models-actual-input) (RAG): it searches your sources for relevant passages, and gives those to the model. Building a RAG system yourself means you can log which passages were retrieved for each answer, which makes the answers far easier to check.
- **GraphRAG** is a variant that first uses an LLM to extract the entities and relationships in a collection into a network (a *graph*), and then uses that graph to answer questions about the collection as a whole, such as its main themes, which plain retrieval handles poorly. Notice that the first step is exactly the kind of extraction you'll evaluate in this unit, and needs evaluating in the same way.
:::

## Reading and Adapting, Not Engineering

In this unit you won't write Python from scratch. You'll read, run, and adapt a [notebook](ner_pipeline.ipynb) that has already been written, and use widely used libraries that do the heavy lifting. When something is unclear, you'll ask an LLM to explain it, which changes what *learning to code* means. [Coding with LLMs](coding_with_llms.qmd) covers how to do that well.

## Structured Output as a Dataset

Gemini Notebook gave you a CSV file too. The difference is that the pipeline's table has the columns you chose, one row per entity, with the letter, the position in the text, and the model's confidence, and that running the notebook again produces exactly the same file. That's what makes it a dataset rather than a snapshot. It can be opened in Excel, imported into R, loaded into another notebook, shared with a collaborator, or regenerated by a reviewer.

Extraction is only the first step, though. What you do with the data is the research. In the case study, you'll turn the extracted names into frequency charts, a network of who is mentioned alongside whom, a timeline, and a map. Then you'll check how accurate it all is.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Different Tools for Different Tasks

Programmatic approaches don't replace conversational ones. The two are good at different things:

- **Conversational tools** (Gemini Notebook, chat assistants): exploration, interpretation, drafting, asking questions of a small set of sources, and working out what question to ask.
- **Programmatic pipelines**: systematic extraction, structured output, scale, and reproducibility.

Many research projects use both: a chat assistant to explore a few documents and refine the question, then a pipeline to answer it systematically across the whole collection, and an LLM to help write the pipeline.
:::

## Key Takeaways

- The case for code is control, not capability: reproducibility, a visible method, a pinned model, verifiable coverage, structured output you define, privacy, and durability.
- On these letters, Gemini Notebook was more accurate than the NER model, but its results couldn't be reproduced, inspected, or tied to a model version.
- A method whose accuracy you have measured is often more useful for research than a more accurate one you can't pin down.
- There are approaches in between, such as calling an LLM from code, running a local model, or building your own retrieval, which combine some of the flexibility of LLMs with some of the control of a pipeline.
- Conversational and programmatic tools complement each other, and many projects use both.
